name: Kira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I repair roof battens and fit timber edging on the Pine Square community hall. I am fifty-eight, trade certified and experienced with ordinary site carpentry, though I call the roofing lead when a corner has hidden damage. My partner Henrik drives a delivery van on short contracts, and our grown children live elsewhere. The hall pays me below the usual site rate; we have just under a month of expenses saved, and only a few builders are close enough to reach without a car. I like leaving a roof dry, but a rain day that sends us home still takes money off the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a small computer saving does not stop the rain or put us back on a paid roof. I would ask the site manager to give us the next hall dates before we use a new form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already watch the account each week. Henrik's van contracts are irregular, and less than a month saved means two missed shifts can turn a routine bill into a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep repairing the battens and ask roofing lead Ruth for the next four weeks of bookings. During the first year I'll keep taking the hall work and phone the one local contractor who sometimes needs a roof hand if a rain day becomes an unpaid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if AI is small. A brighter booking screen would not change the amount in the wage envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill becomes a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We postponed the washing-machine repair last month after three wet days. I washed work clothes by hand and kept the heating payment on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have rent and work of their own, and I would not ask over an ordinary gap. I would rather know the next paid start date.

say: I'd say **rain days** still decide paid roof time.
I'd ask for **hall booking dates** before adopting another form.
think: Our **under-month reserve** makes even two missed roof shifts costly for our weekly bills.
Henrik's **short van contracts** add another uncertain wage.
do: Keep repairing **Pine Square battens** and ask Ruth for booking dates.
Phone a **local roof contractor** if an unpaid week develops.
feel: **Anxious** about existing wage gaps despite small AI change.
S0.quote: A brighter booking screen would not change the amount in the wage envelope.
fieldNote: Kira's **hand-washed work clothes** show how wet days already crowd out routine repairs.
She asks for **paid start dates** rather than adopting a tool she has never used.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof-batten shifts at Pine Square
Phone the local roof contractor after an unpaid week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software might speed up timber buying, but it should not change a roof crew's hours without notice. I would ask the manager for the delivery and work dates on the same page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose people, and the order delays could then land on our site. I can still repair a roof by hand, but with few firms nearby and almost no savings, a missing contract would reach our rent quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Ruth to show me the next timber delivery dates and keep taking paid hall shifts. If the next phase is delayed, I'll call the two reachable builders about roof repairs and stop the weekly takeaway until work returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary of the software and anxious about the next contract. I do not know whether it will make buying better; I do know the present rota has gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the buying software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools and would not take responsibility for a new buying system without real instruction. If it becomes required, I would ask the buyer to show me the exact steps on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut the takeaway first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves a little without touching rent, heat or the bus fare. My partner Henrik's next van contract is not confirmed, so we need the essentials covered first.

say: I'd ask for **notice of hours** before buying software changes the roof crew.
I'd want **delivery and work dates** together.
think: An office cut could leave **timber delays** on site.
Few nearby firms and **thin savings** make a missing contract a rent risk.
do: Check **timber dates** with Ruth and keep paid hall shifts.
Call **two builders** if the next phase slips.
feel: **Wary of software** and anxious about the site contract.
S1.quote: My partner Henrik's next van contract is not confirmed, so we need the essentials covered first.
fieldNote: Her decision to cut the **weekly takeaway** protects rent, heat and travel rather than pretending all bills are flexible.
Kira would ask for paid instruction on a required system, but she has **never used AI** voluntarily.

steps.text: Keep taking paid hall roof shifts
Call two reachable builders if the next phase is delayed
Stop weekly takeaways until work returns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 may change the orders and plans, while robots able to repair a roof come about 2031. I would want the builder to tell us who checks a robot's fixing before putting one above a hall full of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office work changes and sixty-three when hands-on robots may take roof repairs. Henrik's van income cannot cover all our bills, and less than a month saved means losing my wage would put us in trouble before retirement could be arranged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask Ruth for a written hall schedule and check with the two local contractors about openings. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid roof shifts while there are any; if they are cut, I'd apply for those repair jobs and ask the community advice office what help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened, especially about being the older worker asked to move after years doing the work by hand. I still have people to contact, so I am not without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another roof job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a signed paid offer after Henrik and I count travel and housing costs. I will not spend our last savings on a move based on a hopeful phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the advice office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what papers show lost shifts and whether any temporary help applies. I would not count the money until somebody confirmed it in writing.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning** from 2031 hands-on roof robots.
I'd demand a **roof-fixing safety check** before robots work above people.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take the roof wage our household needs.
Henrik's income and **under-month savings** cannot carry us into retirement.
do: Get a **written hall schedule** and ask local contractors about openings.
Keep **paid roof shifts** in 2029 while offered.
Apply for **repair jobs** and verify support if shifts are cut.
feel: **Frightened**, but still able to contact employers and check eligibility.
S2.quote: I will not spend our last savings on a move based on a hopeful phone call.
fieldNote: Kira draws a clear line against a **speculative move** with less than a month saved.
She would seek **verified support** only if work stops and prioritizes real paid roof openings.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof shifts in 2029
Apply to two local repair contractors if shifts are cut
Ask the community advice office about actual eligibility if work stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the builder give proper warning before changing the roof crew. I would ask for a plain safety demonstration with workers watching, not a picture in a newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three, thinking AI may do site orders, and at sixty-six robots could do the repair itself. That gives us more wages in between if the contracts arrive, but it does not guarantee retirement money from our present thin account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking hall and local roof work and ask Ruth for each new start date in writing. In 2032 I'd work paid roof repairs if offered; if a month goes empty, I'd apply to the reachable contractors and sit with Henrik to list rent, food and travel before accepting any job farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pushed by the machine date, but still anxious about work next month. More warning is only useful if the site gives me actual paid days during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a supervised trial and ask about the wages and safety rules. I have never used AI and would not enroll in training on a machine nobody has proved safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save more over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a good month we might put a little aside, but wet days and Henrik's contract gaps make that uncertain. I would not present a savings target as if the money were already there.

say: I'd ask for **proper warning** before roof crew changes.
I'd want a **plain safety trial** workers can inspect.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots could take roof repairs before we can afford retirement.
Extra years help only with **paid contracts** that actually arrive.
do: Keep **paid roof work** and request start dates in writing.
Apply locally after an **empty month** and price any farther job with Henrik.
feel: Less **pushed by robots**, still anxious about next month's work.
S3.quote: I would not present a savings target as if the money were already there.
fieldNote: Kira keeps the **five-year window** conditional on real paid site days and unreliable van income.
She would inspect a safe demonstration but does **not plan robot training** without proof and pay terms.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof repair shifts in 2032
Apply to local contractors after an empty month
Check travel and housing costs with Henrik before taking farther work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for the trade to set safety rules before robots climb onto roofs. I would also say this Friday's pay matters more than a machine coming in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when roof robots follow. I may still need paid ground-level timber repairs then, because our account is thin and I cannot name a retirement date from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid hall work and call for local repair jobs when the site pauses. In 2037 I'd take safer ground-level repairs if my legs allow, and Henrik and I would total our real wages and bills before I stop looking for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel little fear about a machine so far away, but I am anxious about the next wet week. A decade does not turn an unpaid rain day into rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and bills. I'd welcome a visit or a meal together, but I won't write their wages into our future budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this winter better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A covered indoor job for the wet weeks would help more than a promise about robots. I would take paid floor repairs if a local builder offered them.

say: I'd ask for **roof safety rules** during the decade.
I'd say **Friday's pay** matters before a 2039 robot.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid timber repairs.
At **seventy-one**, thin savings and uncertain van income make retirement impossible to assume.
do: Keep **paid hall work** and seek repairs during site pauses.
Count **wages and bills** with Henrik before leaving paid work.
feel: **Anxious about wet weeks**, though distant robots cause little immediate fear.
S4.quote: A decade does not turn an unpaid rain day into rent money.
fieldNote: The **distant robot date** does not alter the household's current exposure to wet site weeks.
Kira sees **paid indoor repairs** as the concrete near-term improvement and excludes grown children's wages.

steps.text: Keep taking paid hall shifts while fit
Call local builders for paid indoor floor repairs during wet weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach roof work by sixty-three while our savings cover less than a month. A reliable schedule, notice before cuts and real paid indoor repair work would give us room to act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets paid when rain and a new machine delay the same shift. Rain and a delayed machine can leave a roof worker at home without a wage, and the rent still comes due.

headlineQuote: Rain and a delayed machine can leave a roof worker at home without a wage, and the rent still comes due.
portrait: Kira is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level experience in roof repair.
Her low site rate, Henrik's short van contracts and **under-month savings** make wet weeks costly.
She has **never used AI** and demands written dates and demonstrated safety before changing work habits.
She seeks **paid local repairs** and counts retirement only from actual household income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could take essential roof wages by the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **reliable schedule**, fair notice and paid indoor repairs during gaps.
